How to read this dashboard

The score

Composite
A 0–100 quality score, weighted technical 40%, fundamental 30%, sentiment 15%, macro 15%. Each block is scored from its own checklist in system-details.md §2. Anything that cannot be measured is excluded and the block renormalised — a missing data feed never counts as a failed test.
Model coverage
How much of the rubric was actually measurable for that name. It tops out below 100% because news sentiment has no data source, and a name can lose more where Yahoo lacks a field for it. Partial coverage can disqualify a candidate but never qualify one — a name needs all four dimensions to be entry-eligible, because price action alone can look excellent while the business deteriorates underneath it.
Verdict
Buy ≥75, Watch 60–74, Ignore <60. This is a verdict on quality, not an instruction to trade. Scoring 75 makes a name eligible to be considered; the entry trigger below decides whether it is actually bought.

The entry trigger

A name is bought only when every one of these is true on the same bar (§3). This is why the "Entries blocked" count is usually far larger than "Actionable entries" — a high score on its own buys nothing.

1. Score
Composite ≥75, with all four dimensions present.
2. Pullback
Price sits 5–10% below its 52-week high. The idea is to buy a shallow dip inside an intact uptrend rather than chase a high or catch a collapse. This is by far the most selective gate — it rejects the large majority of otherwise-qualifying signals.
3. Reversal
The bar shows a hammer, a bullish engulfing, or a narrow-range breakout — evidence the dip is being bought, not still falling.
4. Volume
Volume at least 1.2× its own 20-day average, so the reversal carries participation rather than being a quiet drift.
5. Regime
The market regime permits new longs, and position size is scaled by it.
6. Blackout
No earnings release within 7 days, to avoid holding through a coin-flip.

Signals are evaluated on the close and filled at the next open, never at the price that generated them. Slippage and commission are charged both ways.

Risk and exits

R
The unit of risk: entry price minus the initial stop. Every result here is quoted in R so trades of different sizes compare directly. "Expectancy 0.7R" means the average trade returns 0.7× what it put at risk.
Initial stop
2×ATR(14) below entry, or the last swing low, whichever is nearer — so the stop adapts to each name's own volatility instead of a fixed percentage.
Position size
Risk 1% of equity per trade, capped at 10% of equity in any one name. On large, calm stocks the cap binds first, so realised risk per trade lands well under 1%.
Exits
Stop hit; partial profit at 3R; stop to breakeven after 2R; a time exit after 20 sessions; or a score exit if quality decays below 60.

Reading the backtest

CAGR
The annualised growth rate over the window. The number that matters is not the level but the gap to SPY on the same dates.
Max drawdown
The deepest peak-to-trough fall in equity, as a percent of the peak — the worst stretch an investor would have had to sit through. Lower is normally better, but read it together with mean positions: this strategy's very low drawdown comes mostly from sitting in cash, not from managing risk well. Not participating is not the same as being defensive.
Sharpe
Return per unit of volatility, measured on returns in excess of the risk-free rate. That subtraction is deliberate: most of this portfolio's gain is T-bill interest, and without it the ratio would flatter the strategy for merely holding bills.
Expectancy
Average R per closed trade. Positive expectancy with too few trades still compounds slowly — pair it with the trade count and mean positions.
Win rate
Share of trades that made money. Weak on its own: it says nothing about the size of wins against losses.

Two standing caveats. The backtest universe is today's index, so names that dropped out are invisible and every figure is flattered by survivorship. And only the technical and macro blocks — 55% of the model — participate historically, because point-in-time fundamentals are not available. Read the backtest as a test of the entry, exit and risk mechanics, not as an expected return.

    Replay settings

    Start date

    The replay starts at this close with fresh cash and runs to the latest close on file. Changing it restarts the replay.

    Price colors

    Taiwan and much of East Asia show rising prices in red; the US uses green.

    This replay

    Restart from the same date to test a different plan on identical prices.

    How this desk works

    Every price here is a real closing price from the dashboard's price cache. The clock replays them one session at a time from the start date you choose; you trade at each day's close.

    Costs
    Shorting
    A short credits the sale to your cash and sets aside 50% extra as margin. If your equity falls below 30% of your short positions, the broker buys them back at the close: a margin call.
    Why it moved
    Each day's move is split into the whole market (SPY times the stock's one-year beta), its sector (the sector ETF's move beyond the market), and what is left: the company's own news.
    Two benchmarks
    Pool: buy every pool name priced on the start date, in equal amounts, and do nothing. S&P 500: put the same cash into SPY on the start date and do nothing. Your trades are measured against both: the pool tells you whether trading beat simply owning your own picks, the S&P 500 whether your picks beat the market at all.

    Don't violate the rules

    Scoring, entry, exit and regime rules come from system-details.md. Refresh with the Rescan button when served by python3 dashboard/serve.py, or by hand with python3 -m engine.cli scan --universe data/universe.csv && python3 dashboard/build.py.

    Not financial advice. The backtest is survivorship-biased and covers only the machine-measurable part of the model — read it as a test of the mechanics, not as an expected return.
